title: Addition and contrast
subtitle: as well as, what's more, although, whereas
summary: Add extra information to a sentence, and join two ideas when the second one is surprising.

lesson.heading: Adding information: also, as well, too
lesson.text: The simplest link word is *and*, but we can add more information with **also**, **as well** and **too**. **Also** goes before the main verb or after *be*; **as well** and **too** go at the end.

examples.text: The restaurant has excellent food; it's **also** very good value.
You always get a good view, and the seats are comfortable **as well**.

lesson.heading: as well as, what's more, in addition, besides
lesson.text: These phrases add a second, often stronger, piece of information. **As well as**, **in addition to** and **besides** are followed by a noun or an *-ing* form.

examples.text: **As well as** getting cheaper tickets, I also got the chance to buy them in advance.
The clothes are nice, and **what's more**, the shop is open every day of the week.
The scheme gives young people experience. **In addition**, companies can afford to employ them.
**In addition to** the new food department, they're also planning to open a cafe.
**Besides** being a mum with four children, she's also a successful designer.

lesson.heading: although, despite, in spite of
lesson.text: Use these when the second idea is surprising. **Although** and **even though** are followed by a clause (subject + verb). **Despite** and **in spite of** are followed by a noun, an *-ing* form, or *the fact that*.

examples.text: **Although** the sun was shining, it wasn't very warm.
We found the place quite easily, **even though** we didn't know where it was.
They went for a walk **despite the fact that** it was raining.
**Despite** having no money, he still seemed very happy.
They got there on time **in spite of** the delay.
**In spite of** all the problems, we still enjoyed the trip.

lesson.note: We often add **still** to show that we did not expect this: He didn't do any work but he still passed the exam.

lesson.heading: What comes after the link word
rows: a clause: although we left late
a noun or -ing: despite the rain, in spite of losing
a clause: despite the fact that they were busy
a new sentence or the end of one
a contrasting fact: whereas the others are slow

lesson.heading: however, yet, though
lesson.text: **However** usually links two separate sentences and takes commas. **Yet** joins two parts of one sentence. **Though** is common in speech and usually comes at the end.

examples.text: I don't agree with a lot of his methods. **However**, he is a very good teacher.
We didn't particularly like the house. The garden, **however**, was wonderful.
We went in the autumn, **yet** it was still quite warm.
I didn't like the film much. I'm glad I went to see it, **though**.

lesson.heading: while and whereas
lesson.text: Use **while** and **whereas** to compare two different facts or situations. Both parts of the sentence are true; they are simply different.

examples.text: Alex is very quick to understand, **whereas** the others are quite slow.
I get 20 pounds an hour, **while** Josh only gets 12.
I was very keen on the film, **whereas** Christoph didn't like it at all.

lesson.text: Although + subject and verb; despite / in spite of + noun or -ing. Although it rained = Despite the rain.

exercises.prompt: Does the word add more information, or introduce something surprising?
They enjoyed the course, ___ it was very difficult.
exercises.explanation: Even though is followed by a clause (it was very difficult).

exercises.prompt: It was a fantastic evening, ___ the terrible food.
exercises.explanation: Despite is followed by a noun phrase (the terrible food).

exercises.prompt: I told John the car was too expensive. ___, he still bought it.
exercises.explanation: However links two separate sentences and takes a comma.

exercises.prompt: She's going on holiday with friends. Her parents, ___, are not very happy about it.
exercises.explanation: However can go in the middle of a sentence, between commas.

exercises.prompt: Match each beginning with its ending.

pairs.left: She went to school today although
She always worked hard in class, whereas
pairs.right: most of her classmates were lazy.

pairs.left: She has the ability to do the job. What's more,
She didn't pass the exam in spite of
She worked there for ten years. However,
pairs.right: she was never happy in the job.

exercises.prompt: ___ the fact that they were busy, they still helped us.
exercises.explanation: In spite of / Despite + the fact that + a clause.

exercises.prompt: It's not the best dictionary you can buy. ___, it's better than nothing.
exercises.explanation: However starts a new sentence with a surprising idea.

exercises.prompt: She managed to get there, ___ she didn't have a map like the others.
exercises.explanation: Although / even though is followed by a subject and verb.

exercises.prompt: ___ heavy rain, they've also had very strong winds.
exercises.explanation: In addition to / As well as / Besides + noun adds information.

exercises.prompt: She's the youngest in the group, and she's better than most of them ___.
exercises.explanation: As well and too go at the end of the sentence.

exercises.prompt: I think you can do it. It won't be easy, ___.
exercises.explanation: Though usually comes at the end of a spoken sentence.

exercises.statement: Despite we were on holiday, we decided to work.
exercises.explanation: Despite the fact that we were on holiday, we decided to work. Despite cannot be followed by a clause on its own.
